data.targetWord: The branch of ethics concerned with how humans should relate to and take responsibility for the natural world

examples.en-GB: Environmental ethics asks whether we have a duty to protect the environment for future generations.

data.targetWord: The Christian (and wider religious) concept of responsible management and care of the earth on behalf of God, as a trustee rather than owner

examples.en-GB: Christian stewardship means treating the earth as God's property, not exploiting it for personal gain.

data.targetWord: Meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs

examples.en-GB: Sustainable farming avoids depleting soil and water for short-term gain.

data.targetWord: The Islamic concept of humans as stewards or trustees of Allah's creation, responsible for caring for the earth on God's behalf

examples.en-GB: As khalifah, Muslims are accountable to Allah for how they treat the earth.

data.targetWord: The Islamic concept of excess or waste, which is forbidden; wasting food, water, or resources is considered sinful

examples.en-GB: Israf means Muslims should avoid all unnecessary waste — even wasting water during wudu is condemned.

data.targetWord: The Hindu and Buddhist principle of non-violence towards all living beings, which motivates environmental care and vegetarianism

examples.en-GB: Ahimsa extends to animals and the natural world, motivating many Hindus to avoid harming the environment.

data.targetWord: The Buddhist teaching (pratityasamutpada) that all things arise in connection with each other; nothing exists in isolation, so harming the environment harms all

examples.en-GB: Buddhist interdependence means that destroying a rainforest harms the whole web of life, including humans.

data.targetWord: Long-term changes in global temperature and weather patterns, largely driven by human greenhouse gas emissions

examples.en-GB: Global temperatures have risen approximately 1.2 degrees Celsius since pre-industrial times due to climate change.

data.targetWord: Protecting and preserving natural environments, species, and resources to maintain biodiversity and ecological health

examples.en-GB: Conservation efforts protect endangered species and habitats from destruction.

data.targetWord: The variety of living organisms in a habitat or on Earth; loss of biodiversity weakens ecosystems

examples.en-GB: Biodiversity loss threatens food security and reduces the resilience of natural systems.

data.targetWord: The principle that environmental benefits and harms should be fairly distributed, and that the poorest should not bear a disproportionate burden

examples.en-GB: Environmental justice demands that countries least responsible for climate change should not suffer its worst effects.

data.targetWord: The total greenhouse gas emissions caused by an individual, organisation, or activity, measured in carbon dioxide equivalents

examples.en-GB: Reducing your carbon footprint might involve flying less, eating less meat, or using renewable energy.

data.targetWord: A culture or economic system driven by the purchase and consumption of goods, which can lead to resource depletion and environmental damage

examples.en-GB: Buddhist mindful consumption challenges consumerism by encouraging people to buy only what is needed.

data.targetWord: The Sikh concept of selfless service, which extends to caring for the created world — planting trees, conserving water, and protecting the environment

examples.en-GB: EcoSikh is a Sikh environmental organisation that plants trees as an act of sewa.

data.targetWord: The religious belief that the universe was made by God and is therefore good, valuable, and deserving of care

examples.en-GB: Because creation belongs to God, Christians are called to be stewards — not exploiters — of the natural world.

data.targetWord: The introduction of harmful substances into the environment, damaging ecosystems, wildlife, and human health

examples.en-GB: Approximately 8 million tonnes of plastic enters the oceans annually, causing serious marine pollution.

data.targetWord: People who will live after us; a key reason for environmental responsibility is the ethical obligation to leave a liveable world for those who come after

examples.en-GB: The Humanist argument for environmental care focuses on our obligations to future generations.

data.targetWord: The Buddhist practice of buying and using only what is genuinely needed, rather than what craving and desire demand

examples.en-GB: Mindful consumption means choosing second-hand goods and avoiding unnecessary purchases.

data.targetWord: The Islamic concept of balance in creation; Allah created the world in perfect balance, and humans must not disturb it through waste or destruction

examples.en-GB: The Qur'anic concept of mizan means humans have a duty to maintain the balance of the natural world.

data.targetWord: The moral duty to care for the environment — whether grounded in religious obligation, concern for future generations, or reason and empathy

examples.en-GB: Religious and non-religious people reach similar conclusions about environmental responsibility through different foundations.

The Hindu principle of non-violence towards all living beings, which motivates environmental care, is called ____.
The Buddhist teaching that all things arise in connection with each other and nothing exists in isolation is called ____.
Meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their needs is called ____.
Long-term changes in global temperature driven by human greenhouse gas emissions is called ____ change.
The fair distribution of environmental harms and benefits across communities is called environmental ____.
The Sikh concept of selfless service, which extends to caring for creation, is called ____.
The total greenhouse gas emissions caused by a person or activity is called a carbon ____.
The variety of living organisms in a habitat or on Earth is called ____.
The Buddhist practice of buying and using only what is genuinely needed is called ____ consumption.
The Islamic concept of balance in creation — which humans must not disturb — is called ____.
Protecting and preserving natural environments and species is called ____.
A culture or economic system driven by the constant purchase of goods is called ____.

data.title: Arrange the steps from individual belief to environmental action in the correct order
items: A religious or ethical belief (e.g. stewardship, khalifah, ahimsa) is held
The belief is applied to the question of environmental care
A personal action or lifestyle choice is made (e.g. reduced waste, vegetarianism)
The individual advocates for or inspires collective and structural change

data.title: Put the stages of the environmental responsibility chain in the correct order
items: God (or nature/future generations) creates or values the natural world
The natural world is entrusted to human care
Humans make individual and collective choices about how to treat the environment
Those choices have consequences for future generations and all living beings

data.title: Arrange the following environmental challenges from local to global scale
items: Wasting food at home — individual household level
A local factory polluting a river — community level
A country's fossil fuel use affecting its own air quality — national level
Global greenhouse gas emissions causing worldwide climate change — international level
